# Common Data Formats & Public Repositories {#sec-appendix-data-formats}

This appendix is a **field guide** to the file formats you will meet most often as a bioengineer working with data, and to the public repositories where published datasets, sequences, genomes, and structures live. It is meant to be scanned in about 15 minutes and returned to whenever you open an unfamiliar file or need to find a published dataset.

::: callout-note
**Why an appendix and not a tutorial?** Recognizing file formats and navigating data repositories is a **skill** more than a procedure: every repository's interface evolves, and the right portal depends on your question. The command-line tools used here (`head`, `zcat`, `grep`, `wc`, `wget`) are introduced in @sec-unix-fundamentals and Lectures 03-05; see @sec-grep-regex for more `grep`. Terms are defined in the the Glossary (@sec-appendix-glossary).
:::

# Part 1 - Common file formats {#file-formats}

A useful first question for any file: **is it plain text or binary?** Plain-text files can be inspected with `head`, `less`, and `grep`, versioned with Git, and read by any language decades from now. Binary files are smaller and faster but need specific software to open.

```bash
file mystery_data.dat     # the `file` command guesses the type
head -n 5 mystery_data.dat  # plain text shows readable lines; binary shows gibberish
```

## Plain-text tables: CSV and TSV {#sec-csv-tsv}

The workhorse of scientific data exchange. Each line is a row; columns are separated by commas (**CSV**, `.csv`) or tab characters (**TSV**, `.tsv` or `.txt`).

```
sample_id,material,stiffness_kPa,temp_C
S01,PEG_hydrogel,12.4,37
S02,PEG_hydrogel,13.1,37
S03,alginate,8.7,37
```

- The first line is usually a **header** with column names.
- Follow **tidy data** conventions (Lecture 02): one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell.
- TSV is safer when text fields might contain commas (e.g., gene descriptions).
- Read in R with `readr::read_csv()` / `read_tsv()`; in Python with `pandas.read_csv()` (add `sep="\t"` for TSV).
- Quick shell checks: `head file.csv`, `wc -l file.csv` (rows + header), `cut -d, -f3 file.csv | sort | uniq -c` (tabulate column 3).

## Spreadsheets: Excel (.xlsx) and its caveats {#sec-excel}

Excel is fine for viewing and data entry, but it is risky as the *only* copy of your data:

- **Automatic conversion**: Excel silently converts some values. Gene symbols such as *SEPT2*, *MARCH1*, and *DEC1* have been turned into dates ("2-Sep", "1-Mar"), and long numeric IDs are converted to scientific notation, losing digits. A 2016 survey found these errors in roughly one-fifth of papers with supplementary Excel gene lists (Ziemann et al., *Genome Biology*, https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-016-1044-7); HGNC later renamed several genes partly because of this. Keeping raw data in plain text and doing all manipulation in code is one of the core recommendations of "good enough" scientific computing practice [@wilson2017good].
- **Hidden structure**: merged cells, colors used as data, multiple tables per sheet, and formulas make files hard to read programmatically.
- **Proprietary binary format**: `.xlsx` is a zipped XML bundle, so Git cannot show meaningful diffs.

::: callout-tip
**Keep a CSV copy.** Treat raw data as read-only, store a plain-text CSV (one sheet = one CSV) alongside any `.xlsx`, and do analysis in code. If you must import into Excel, use **Data → From Text/CSV** and set gene-name or ID columns to **Text**. In R, `readxl::read_excel()` reads `.xlsx` directly without Excel.
:::

## Sequences: FASTA {#sec-fasta}

Plain text for DNA, RNA, or protein sequences. Each record is a **header line starting with `>`** followed by one or more lines of sequence:

```
>NM_000546.6 Homo sapiens tumor protein p53 (TP53), mRNA
CTCAAAAGTCTAGAGCCACCGTCCAGGGAGCAGGTAGCTGCTGGGCTCCGGGGACACTTTGCGTTCGGGC
TGGGAGCGTGCTTTCCACGACGGTGACACGCTTCCCTGGATTGGCAGCCAGACTGCCTTCCGGGTCACTG
>sp|P04637|P53_HUMAN Cellular tumor antigen p53
MEEPQSDPSVEPPLSQETFSDLWKLLPENNVLSPLPSQAMDDLMLSPDDIEQWFTEDPGP
```

- Extensions: `.fa`, `.fasta`, `.fna` (nucleotide), `.faa` (amino acid), often gzipped (`.fa.gz`).
- Used for reference genomes, transcripts, primers, and protein sequences.
- No quality scores (contrast with FASTQ).
- Count records: `grep -c '>' file.fasta`. List headers: `grep '>' file.fasta | head`.

## Raw sequencing reads: FASTQ {#sec-fastq}

Plain text with a strict **4-line-per-read** structure (@tbl-fastq-record):

```
@SRR12345.1 NS500126:1:H7TG3BGXY:1:11101:18923:1057
NCATGCAGCGTACGGTAATTGGCAGGCATTAGCAGCATCC
+
#AAAAFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF
```

| Line | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Header: read ID plus instrument, run, lane, tile, and x/y position. Starts with `@` |
| 2 | The **sequence** (A/C/G/T/N) |
| 3 | A `+` separator (sometimes repeats the header) |
| 4 | **Per-base quality scores**, one ASCII character per base, same length as line 2 |

: The four lines of a FASTQ record {#tbl-fastq-record}

::: {.callout-note title="Key concept - Phred quality scores"}
Each quality character encodes a **Phred score** $Q = -10 \log_{10}(P)$, where $P$ is the probability that the base call is wrong (@tbl-phred-scores):

| Phred Q | Error probability | Base-call accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 1 in 10 | 90% |
| 20 | 1 in 100 | 99% |
| 30 | 1 in 1,000 | 99.9% |
| 40 | 1 in 10,000 | 99.99% |

: Phred quality scores and the base-call accuracy they encode {#tbl-phred-scores}

Modern Illumina data use **Phred+33** encoding: the character's ASCII code minus 33 gives Q. So `!` (ASCII 33) is Q0, `+` (43) is Q10, `5` (53) is Q20, `?` (63) is Q30, and `I` (73) is Q40. In the example above, the leading `#` (Q2) on the `N` base signals a very low-confidence call.
:::

- Paired-end runs produce two files per sample, typically `..._R1_001.fastq.gz` and `..._R2_001.fastq.gz`; the reads in each file are in the same order.
- Because each read is exactly 4 lines, **number of reads = lines / 4**: `echo $(( $(zcat reads.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))`.
- Quality-control tools such as FastQC summarize quality scores across a whole file.

## Compressed files (.gz) and streaming {#sec-gzip-streaming}

Sequencing and other large text files are almost always stored **gzip-compressed** (`.gz`), often 3-5x smaller. You rarely need to decompress them to disk; instead **stream** them through a pipe:

```bash
zcat reads.fastq.gz | head -n 8          # first two reads
zcat reads.fastq.gz | wc -l              # total lines
zcat genome.fa.gz | grep -c '>'          # number of sequences
zless annotation.gtf.gz                  # page through interactively

gzip results.tsv                         # compress (creates results.tsv.gz, removes original)
gunzip results.tsv.gz                    # decompress
gzip -k results.tsv                      # -k keeps the original
```

On macOS, the built-in `zcat` expects `.Z` files; use `gzcat file.gz` or `zcat < file.gz` instead. Some genomics files use **bgzip** (block gzip), which is still readable with `zcat` but also allows indexed random access (e.g., with `tabix` or `samtools`). Other archive types you will see: `.zip` (`unzip`), `.tar.gz`/`.tgz` (`tar -xzf file.tar.gz`), and `.bz2` (`bzcat`).

## Alignments: SAM and BAM {#sec-sam-bam}

When reads are aligned to a reference genome, the result is stored as **SAM** (Sequence Alignment/Map; tab-delimited text with a `@` header section and one line per alignment) or its compressed binary equivalent **BAM** (`.bam`, with an index `.bai`). Use `samtools` [@li2009samtools; @danecek2021twelve] to work with them (its sibling `bcftools` does the same for VCF):

```bash
samtools view -H sample.bam | head       # header lines
samtools view sample.bam | head -n 3     # first 3 alignments as SAM text
samtools flagstat sample.bam             # summary: how many reads mapped
```

## Genomic annotation and interval formats {#sec-genomic-annotation-and-interval-formats}

All are tab-delimited text, one feature per line; chromosome names must match the reference genome you use.

- **GFF3 / GTF** (`.gff3`, `.gtf`): nine columns describing genes, transcripts, exons, and CDS features, 1-based coordinates. Reference annotation sets such as GENCODE [@frankish2021gencode] and Ensembl are distributed in this form.

  ```
  chr17  HAVANA  gene  7661779  7687538  .  -  .  gene_id "ENSG00000141510"; gene_name "TP53";
  ```

- **BED** (`.bed`): at minimum chromosome, start, end; used for regions, peaks, and targets. **0-based, half-open** coordinates (start is counted from 0 and the end position is excluded).

  ```
  chr17  7661778  7687538  TP53  0  -
  ```

- **VCF** (`.vcf`, `.vcf.gz`): genetic variants (SNPs, indels) relative to a reference, with `##` metadata lines, a `#CHROM` header, and optional per-sample genotype columns.

  ```
  #CHROM  POS      ID         REF  ALT  QUAL  FILTER  INFO
  chr17   7675088  rs28934578 C    T    60    PASS    DP=42
  ```

## Hierarchical binary data: HDF5, .h5, and .h5ad {#sec-hdf5}

**HDF5** (Hierarchical Data Format 5; `.h5`, `.hdf5`) stores many large numerical arrays and their metadata inside a single binary file organized like a file system (groups and datasets). It supports compression and lets programs read just the slice they need without loading the whole file, so it is common for microscopy and imaging data, simulation output, instrument data, and large matrices. `.h5ad` is the HDF5-based file format for Python's **AnnData** package, widely used for large annotated matrices (e.g., samples/cells by genes).

- Inspect from the shell with `h5ls -r file.h5` (from the HDF5 tools).
- Read in Python with `h5py` (or `anndata.read_h5ad()` for `.h5ad`); in R with the Bioconductor `rhdf5` package.

## R objects: .rds and .RData vs plain text {#sec-rds-rdata}

- `saveRDS(obj, "file.rds")` / `readRDS("file.rds")` saves and restores **one** R object exactly (including factor levels, attributes, and complex objects such as model fits).
- `save(a, b, file = "file.RData")` / `load("file.RData")` stores **several** objects and restores them under their original names (which can silently overwrite objects in your session).

Both are convenient for **work in progress** and for passing results between steps of your own pipeline, but they are **not good archival or sharing formats**: they are readable only by R, can break across major package versions, and cannot be diffed in Git. For anything you will share, publish, or keep long-term, **also write a plain-text version** (`readr::write_csv()`) and keep the code that regenerates the R object. Avoid saving your whole workspace to `.RData` at exit (set "Save workspace" to **Never**). See @sec-r-programming and @sec-appendix-r.

## Structured text: JSON and YAML {#sec-json-yaml}

Both represent nested key-value data in plain text and are common for configuration files, metadata, pipeline parameters, and web APIs.

**JSON** (`.json`) uses braces, brackets, and quoted keys:

```json
{
  "experiment": "hydrogel_swelling",
  "temperature_C": 37,
  "replicates": [1, 2, 3],
  "instrument": {"name": "rheometer", "geometry": "parallel plate"}
}
```

**YAML** (`.yml`, `.yaml`) expresses the same structure with indentation, and is what Quarto uses for document headers and `_quarto.yml` project files (@sec-quarto-documents):

```yaml
experiment: hydrogel_swelling
temperature_C: 37
replicates: [1, 2, 3]
instrument:
  name: rheometer
  geometry: parallel plate
```

YAML is whitespace-sensitive: use spaces (never tabs) and keep indentation consistent. Read JSON with `jsonlite` in R or the `json` module in Python; `jq` is a handy command-line JSON tool. Many pipelines write a `params.json` or `config.yaml` describing a run; archive it with your outputs as the "lab notebook entry" for your computational analysis.

## Format quick reference {#sec-format-quick-reference}

@tbl-format-quick-reference summarizes the formats above and the tools for inspecting each.

| Extension | Type | What it holds | Look inside with |
|---|---|---|---|
| `.csv`, `.tsv` | text | Tables | `head`, `less`, R/Python |
| `.xlsx` | binary (zipped XML) | Spreadsheets | Excel, `readxl`; keep a CSV copy |
| `.fa`, `.fasta` | text | Sequences (no qualities) | `head`, `grep -c '>'` |
| `.fastq.gz` | compressed text | Reads + quality scores | `zcat \| head` |
| `.sam` / `.bam` | text / binary | Read alignments | `samtools view` |
| `.gtf`, `.gff3`, `.bed`, `.vcf` | text | Annotations, intervals, variants | `head`, `grep`, `zless` |
| `.h5`, `.h5ad` | binary | Large arrays / annotated matrices | `h5ls`, `h5py`, `rhdf5` |
| `.rds`, `.RData` | binary | R objects | `readRDS()`, `load()` |
| `.json`, `.yaml` | text | Configuration, metadata | `cat`, `jq` |

: Quick reference to common bioengineering data formats {#tbl-format-quick-reference}

# Part 2 - Public data repositories

Journals and funders increasingly require that data be deposited in a public repository, and published data are a free resource for learning, method development, and comparison with your own results. Most biological repositories belong to a small set of international organizations that mirror each other.

## NCBI (US National Center for Biotechnology Information) {#sec-ncbi}

- [**GEO**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) (Gene Expression Omnibus): processed functional-genomics data (expression tables, count matrices, sample metadata) from microarray and sequencing studies [@barrett2013geo]. Series have `GSE######` accessions, and each sample has a `GSM######` record. When a paper says *"data are available at GEO under GSE#####"*, open the series page, check the sample list, and scroll to **Supplementary file** to download. In R, the Bioconductor **GEOquery** package (`getGEO()`, `getGEOSuppFiles()`) retrieves these directly.
- [**SRA**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra) (Sequence Read Archive) [@leinonen2011sra]: **raw** sequencing reads (FASTQ/BAM). Accessions: `SRR` (run), `SRX` (experiment), `SRP` (study). Use it when you need to re-process data from scratch. Files are **big** (often several to tens of GB per sample), so plan storage (e.g., Talapas project or scratch space, Lecture 08) before downloading.
- [**GenBank / RefSeq**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore): GenBank is the archive of all submitted nucleotide sequences; **RefSeq** is NCBI's curated, non-redundant set of reference sequences (accessions like `NM_` for mRNA, `NP_` for protein, `NC_` for chromosomes). Download records as FASTA from the page's **Send to** menu or with NCBI's `datasets` command-line tool.
- [**BioProject / BioSample**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/): the umbrella records that tie a study (`PRJNA…`) and its biological samples (`SAMN…`) to the associated GEO, SRA, and GenBank entries.

::: callout-tip
**Getting raw reads.** Two practical routes:

-   **`sra-tools`** on the command line: `prefetch SRR12345678` then `fasterq-dump --split-files SRR12345678` (gives paired `_1.fastq` and `_2.fastq`). On Talapas, look for it with `module spider sra-tools`, or install it with conda/Bioconda.
-   **[SRA Explorer](https://sra-explorer.info/)**: paste in an accession and it returns ready-to-use `wget`/`curl` download commands, usually pointing at the ENA mirror.
:::

## EBI / ENA (Europe) {#sec-ebi-ena}

The [European Bioinformatics Institute](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/) runs the European counterparts: the [**European Nucleotide Archive (ENA)**](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/) mirrors SRA and GenBank (the same `SRR…` accessions work) and often provides direct FTP/HTTPS links to FASTQ files that you can `wget` without `sra-tools`. [**BioStudies / ArrayExpress**](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/) is the European counterpart to GEO, and [**UniProt**](https://www.uniprot.org/) is the central resource for protein sequences and functional annotation.

## Reference genomes and annotations: UCSC and Ensembl {#sec-ucsc-ensembl}

- [**UCSC Genome Browser**](https://genome.ucsc.edu/): interactive browser for genomes and annotation tracks, plus bulk downloads of genome FASTA, annotation files, and the Table Browser for exporting regions as BED/GTF. Assemblies are named like `hg38` (human) or `mm39` (mouse).
- [**Ensembl**](https://www.ensembl.org/): genome browser and annotation database with stable gene IDs (`ENSG…`) and a public [FTP site](https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/) for genome FASTA and GTF/GFF3 files for hundreds of vertebrate species (plus [Ensembl Genomes](https://ensemblgenomes.org/) for plants, fungi, bacteria, and invertebrates).

Always record **which assembly and annotation release** you used (e.g., GRCh38, Ensembl release number), because coordinates and gene models change between versions. Note also that UCSC names chromosomes `chr1` while Ensembl uses `1`.

## Protein structures: Protein Data Bank {#sec-protein-structures-protein-data-bank}

The [**RCSB Protein Data Bank (PDB)**](https://www.rcsb.org/) archives experimentally determined 3D structures of proteins, nucleic acids, and complexes, each with a four-character ID (e.g., `1TUP`). Download coordinates as `.pdb` or the newer `.cif` (mmCIF) text formats; view them in the browser, or in tools like PyMOL or ChimeraX. The [AlphaFold Protein Structure Database](https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/) provides predicted structures for most known proteins.

## General-purpose repositories: Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad {#sec-general-repositories}

For data that do not fit a specialized repository (imaging, mechanical testing, simulation output, code, and supplementary tables), general-purpose repositories assign each deposit a permanent **DOI** so it can be cited:

- [**Zenodo**](https://zenodo.org/) (run by CERN): free; integrates with GitHub to archive a tagged release of a code repository with a DOI.
- [**Figshare**](https://figshare.com/): used by many journals for supplementary data.
- [**Dryad**](https://datadryad.org/): curated repository for data underlying publications, common in ecology, evolution, and biology.

## How to choose {#sec-how-to-choose}

@tbl-repository-choice matches common needs to the repository that serves them.

| If you want... | Go to... |
|---|---|
| Processed expression data / count tables from a paper | **GEO** (or BioStudies/ArrayExpress) |
| Raw sequencing reads (FASTQ) | **SRA** or **ENA** (via `sra-tools` or SRA Explorer) |
| A specific gene, mRNA, or protein sequence | **GenBank/RefSeq**, **UniProt** |
| A reference genome FASTA + GTF annotation | **Ensembl** or **UCSC** |
| To see what samples belong to a study | **BioProject / BioSample** |
| A 3D protein structure | **PDB** (experimental), **AlphaFold DB** (predicted) |
| Imaging, mechanical, simulation, or other non-sequence data with a DOI | **Zenodo**, **Figshare**, **Dryad** |
| To publish and cite your own code | GitHub + **Zenodo** release (@sec-git-github) |

: Which public repository to use for which kind of data {#tbl-repository-choice}

## FAIR Data and Public Repositories {#sec-fair-data}

Everything above is about *finding and reading* other people's data. Sooner or later you will be on the other side: a journal, a funder (the NIH Data Management and Sharing Policy applies to all NIH-funded work since 2023), or a collaborator will ask for yours. Done well, sharing produces citations (reanalysis papers cite their input datasets), a one-line answer to "can I see your raw data?", and compliance that passes review. Done poorly, the dataset sits on a lab drive until it is unreadable. The cost of doing it well is paid up front, during the project; the payoff lasts the lifetime of the data.

### The FAIR Principles {#sec-the-fair-principles}

Wilkinson et al. [@wilkinson2016fair] proposed four principles for data that people *and machines* can reuse (@tbl-fair-principles).

| Principle | One-line definition | What it means for you |
|---|---|---|
| **F**indable | Data and metadata have a persistent identifier and are indexed in a searchable registry | Get an accession (GEO, SRA, BioProject) or a DOI (Zenodo, Dryad); a lab website is not enough |
| **A**ccessible | Anyone (or anyone authorized) can retrieve the data by that identifier through an open, standard protocol | HTTPS/FTP download; controlled access is fine for sensitive human data, as long as the *procedure* is open |
| **I**nteroperable | Data use shared formats and controlled vocabularies so datasets combine cleanly | CSV/FASTA/FASTQ rather than proprietary formats; standard units; ontology terms rather than free text |
| **R**eusable | Provenance, a clear license, and enough metadata for someone else to reanalyze | README, data dictionary, software versions, license file |

: The four FAIR principles [@wilkinson2016fair] and their practical consequences {#tbl-fair-principles}

FAIR is not the same as *open*: patient genomes in a controlled-access archive can satisfy all four criteria. The principle most datasets fail is **I**: "B cells" in a free-text column is a different string from "B-cell", "Bcell", and "B_cell" to a computer, so every downstream integration needs a human to reconcile terms. The most common *omission* is **F**: data deposited without a stable identifier, or not indexed where searchers look.

### Where Data Go: The NCBI Hierarchy {#sec-where-data-go-the-ncbi-hierarchy}

For sequencing-based studies the canonical archive is NCBI (mirrored by EBI/ENA), and its records nest (@tbl-ncbi-hierarchy). The same structure applies to bulk RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, genome resequencing, microbiome amplicons, and any other sequencing assay.

| Record | Accession | What it holds | How many |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BioProject** | `PRJNA######` | The study as a whole: title, abstract, grant, publication | One per paper |
| **BioSample** | `SAMN########` | One biological sample: organism, tissue, donor or strain, treatment, collection date | One per sample |
| **SRA** run | `SRR#######` | The raw reads (FASTQ or BAM) from one sequencing run, linked to its BioSample [@leinonen2011sra] | One or more per sample |
| **GEO** series / sample | `GSE######` / `GSM######` | *Processed* expression data: count matrices, normalized tables, and the sample metadata; GEO creates the SRA and BioSample records for you when you submit expression data [@barrett2013geo] | One series per study, one GSM per sample |

: The NCBI record hierarchy for sequencing data {#tbl-ncbi-hierarchy}

The submission order follows the hierarchy: create the BioProject, register BioSamples, upload raw reads to SRA (each run linked to its `SAMN`), then, for expression studies, submit processed data and metadata to GEO, which links back to the BioProject and SRA runs. Cite every accession in the paper's *Data Availability* statement. Non-sequencing data (imaging, mechanical testing, simulations, code) go to a general-purpose repository with a DOI (Zenodo, Figshare, Dryad, above).

### The Canonical Sample Sheet {#sec-the-canonical-sample-sheet}

Most of the work of sharing is metadata, and the discipline that makes it painless is a single **canonical sample sheet**, started at experimental design time and kept under version control alongside your code. "Sample 1, Sample 2, Sample 3" is not metadata; at minimum the sheet answers who or what the sample came from, what tissue or material, what condition or treatment, what protocol, who processed it, when, on what instrument, with what software version. Its rules:

- **One row per sample, one column per variable** (this is @sec-tidy-data applied to your experiment).
- **A stable, unique `sample_id`** that never changes and appears in every file name, every FASTQ header you can control, and every downstream table. NCBI links BioSample, SRA, and GEO records by this ID, and the match is case-sensitive and literal: `donor1_CTRL` and `Donor1_CTRL` will not link. Manual retyping of sample names across three submission spreadsheets is the single most common cause of broken submissions.
- **Controlled vocabularies, not free text**, for anything you will filter or join on: fixed spellings for conditions (`control`/`treated`, not `ctrl`, `Control`, `CTRL`), standard units in the column name (`stiffness_kPa`), ISO dates (`2026-03-14`), and, where an ontology exists, its term ID (Uberon for tissues, NCBI Taxonomy for organisms, Cell Ontology for cell types, EFO for assays; look them up at the [Ontology Lookup Service](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ols4/)).
- **Metadata columns for every batch effect** you can record: extraction date, library prep kit and lot, sequencing run, operator. You cannot correct for a batch you did not write down.

```
sample_id      donor_id  tissue_ontology  condition  replicate  extraction_date  library_kit     run_id
donor1_ctrl    D001      UBERON:0000178   control    1          2026-02-03       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0412
donor1_treat   D001      UBERON:0000178   treated    1          2026-02-03       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0412
donor2_ctrl    D002      UBERON:0000178   control    2          2026-02-10       TruSeq_v2_lot7  RUN_0413
```

At submission time every upload template (BioSample, SRA, GEO) is *derived programmatically* from this one sheet with a few lines of `dplyr::transmute()` or pandas, so that names, dates, and IDs appear in exactly one place and inconsistencies are fixed there and propagate everywhere.

### Plan Sharing at Design Time {#sec-plan-sharing-at-design-time}

The biggest mistake is thinking about deposition only when the manuscript is in revision. By then the sample metadata is scattered across several lab notebooks, the ontology terms have to be reconstructed from memory, and the person who ran the samples has graduated. Instead, at design time:

1. Start the canonical sample sheet with every column deposition will need, and update it as samples arrive.
2. Decide *which* repositories the data will go to and check their required metadata fields now, not later.
3. Keep raw data read-only in a clearly named directory (@sec-talapas-storage) and never edit it in place.
4. Record software versions and parameters for every processing step in the analysis code or a `config.yaml` (above).

### Checksums, README, Data Dictionary, License {#sec-data-sharing-checklist}

Four small files travel with a well-shared dataset.

**Checksums** prove that a file arrived intact. Compute one when you create or download a file and compare it after every transfer (repositories publish theirs; SRA and ENA list MD5 sums per file):

```bash
md5sum sample_R1.fastq.gz                    # prints a 32-character fingerprint
md5sum *.fastq.gz > checksums.md5             # record fingerprints for a directory
md5sum -c checksums.md5                       # later, or on another machine: verify
```

On macOS use `md5 file` or `shasum -a 256 file`. A single changed byte, a truncated download, or a job killed mid-write (see @sec-right-sizing) produces a different checksum, which is far easier to notice than a subtly corrupt file.

A **README** (plain text or Markdown, at the top of the dataset) says what the data are, who generated them, when, with what instrument and protocol, how the files are organized, and how to cite them. A **data dictionary** describes every column of every table: name, meaning, type, units, allowed values, and how missing values are coded. Together they are what turns a directory of files into something a stranger can use.

A **license** states what others may do with the data; without one, reuse is legally ambiguous even if the files are public. Common choices are CC0 (public domain, the default at many repositories and the simplest for data) and CC BY (reuse with attribution); code is usually released under a software license such as MIT or GPL instead. Human-subject data may need a data-use agreement rather than an open license; your IRB and repository will say which.

::: callout-tip
**A minimal FAIR checklist for any dataset.** A persistent identifier (accession or DOI); open, plain-text formats where possible; a canonical sample sheet with stable IDs and controlled vocabularies; a README and data dictionary; recorded software versions; checksums; and a license. See also the [GO FAIR initiative](https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/).
:::

# Part 3 - A short hands-on exercise

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1 - download a FASTA file and count sequences"}
Run these commands in a terminal (macOS, Linux, WSL, or Talapas). They download the complete set of predicted protein sequences for baker's yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*) from Ensembl, a small (about 2 MB) gzipped FASTA file. (On macOS, replace `zcat` with `gzcat`, and use `curl -L -O <url>` if `wget` is not installed.)

```bash
mkdir -p ~/data_practice && cd ~/data_practice

wget https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/current_fasta/saccharomyces_cerevisiae/pep/Saccharomyces_cerevisiae.R64-1-1.pep.all.fa.gz

ls -lh                                   # how big is the compressed file?
zcat Saccharomyces_cerevisiae.R64-1-1.pep.all.fa.gz | head -n 5
zcat Saccharomyces_cerevisiae.R64-1-1.pep.all.fa.gz | grep -c '>'
```

1.  How many protein sequences are in the file?
2.  Use `grep` to find the header line(s) for a gene you know (e.g., `grep 'CDC28'`). What information does the header contain?
3.  Decompress with `gunzip -k` and compare file sizes with `ls -lh`. What is the compression ratio?

If the URL has changed, browse <https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/current_fasta/> to find the current file name; checking and adapting a URL like this is a normal part of working with public data.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 2 - explore a GEO series"}
1.  Go to <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/> and search for a topic related to your research (e.g., *"hydrogel mesenchymal stem cells"* or *"cardiomyocyte mechanical stretch"*). Filter to **Series**.
2.  Open one `GSE` record. What organism and platform were used? How many samples (`GSM` records)?
3.  Scroll to **Supplementary file**. What formats are the processed data in (`.csv.gz`, `.txt.gz`, `.xlsx`, `.h5`)? Download one with `wget` (right-click the **(http)** link to copy its URL) and inspect it with `zcat file | head`.
4.  Follow the **SRA Run Selector** link. How many runs are there, and how large is the raw data in total? Paste one `SRR` accession into [SRA Explorer](https://sra-explorer.info/) to see the download commands (you do not need to run them).
5.  Is the dataset FAIR? Note one thing the authors did well and one thing that made reuse harder (missing units, unclear column names, Excel-only files, etc.).
:::

-   The Glossary (@sec-appendix-glossary) and the [Resources hub](../../Resources.html).
-   The [hts-specs](https://samtools.github.io/hts-specs/) pages: official specifications for SAM/BAM, VCF, and related formats.
-   UCSC, [Data file formats FAQ](https://genome.ucsc.edu/FAQ/FAQformat.html): concise descriptions of BED, GFF/GTF, and many other genomics formats.
-   NCBI, [GEO documentation](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/info/) and [SRA documentation](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra/docs/).
-   Broman & Woo, "Data Organization in Spreadsheets," *The American Statistician* (2018), https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2017.1375989: practical rules for spreadsheets that stay analyzable.
-   Wilson et al., "Good enough practices in scientific computing," *PLOS Computational Biology* (2017) [@wilson2017good].
-   Wilkinson et al., "The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship," *Scientific Data* (2016) [@wilkinson2016fair].
